en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Acelaka Chapter 41. The Training Rule on the Naked Ascetics.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Now at that time, there was an abundance of fresh food for the Saṅgha.
Then the Venerable Ānanda informed the Blessed One of this matter. “In that case, Ānanda, give some cake to the leftovers-eaters,” he said.

“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Having assented, he had the leftovers-eaters sit down in order and began giving them cake one by one; however, thinking one [person] was a certain female wanderer, he gave her two cakes.
The female wanderers around her said to that wanderer, "This ascetic is your lover.
"That ascetic is not my lover; thinking there was one, he gave me two cakes," she replied.
A second time... [and so on].
A third time, the Venerable Ānanda, giving out one cake at a time, gave two cakes to that same female wanderer, thinking there was only one.
The other female wanderers said to her, "This ascetic is your lover.
She replied, "That ascetic is not my lover; he gave me two cakes, thinking there was only one."
“They are a paramour, not a paramour! they quarreled.
Then a certain Ājīvaka went to the food-distribution area.
A certain bhikkhu, having mixed rice with abundant ghee, gave a large alms-meal to that Ājīvaka.
Then that Ājīvaka, taking that alms-food, departed.
Another Ājīvaka said this to him: "Friend, where did you obtain this alms-food?
"Friend, it was obtained from the meal distribution of that shaven-headed householder, the ascetic Gotama."
The lay followers heard this conversation between those Ājīvakas.

Then those lay followers approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those lay followers said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, these sectarians desire disrepute for the Buddha, they desire disrepute for the Dhamma, and they desire disrepute for the Saṅgha.”
"It would be well, venerable sir, if the masters did not give with their own hands to the members of other sects.
Then the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened those lay followers with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then those lay followers, having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma...
Having been thus encouraged, they rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him with their right side toward him, and departed.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this context, having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the bhikkhus:
"Therefore, bhikkhus, I shall lay down a training rule for the bhikkhus based on ten reasons."
For the well-being of the Saṅgha, for the comfort of the Saṅgha... [and so on] ...for the endurance of the true Dhamma, and for the support of the Vinaya.
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whichever monk, however, should give hard food or soft food with his own hand to a naked ascetic, or to a male wanderer, or to a female wanderer, it is an offense entailing expiation.”
"But whoever" means whoever such a person...
"a bhikkhu" means a monk.
... [as before] ... this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu.
One called a naked ascetic (acelaka) is anyone who has entered the life of a wanderer and goes about naked.
A "wanderer" (paribbājaka) is anyone who has entered the state of a wanderer, excluding both monks (bhikkhu) and novices (sāmaṇera).
A "female wanderer" (paribbājikā) is...
Except for a bhikkhunī, a sikkhamānā, and a sāmaṇerī, any woman who has entered the life of a wanderer.
"Hard food" means the five kinds of cooked food; excluding water and tooth-sticks, the remainder is called hard food.
"Eatable food" means the five kinds of cooked food: boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, and meat.
"Should give" means...
If one gives with the body, or with what is connected to the body, or with what is relinquishable, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one gives hard food or soft food with one's own hand to a member of another sect while perceiving them to be a member of another sect, there is an offense of expiation.
If one gives hard food or soft food with one's own hand to a member of another sect while being uncertain of it, there is an offense of expiation.
If one gives hard food or soft food with one's own hand to a non-Tīrthika while perceiving them as a non-Tīrthika, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one gives water or a tooth-stick, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one gives to a non-Tīrthika while perceiving them as a Tīrthika, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not a non-Buddhist and one is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is not a non-Buddhist and one perceives it as such, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
He causes [another] to give but does not give himself;
he gives after having set it aside;
he gives an external ointment.
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of the first offender.
The first training rule on naked ascetics is concluded.
